aiOverview.content: A pied-à-terre tax is a proposed annual surcharge on luxury second homes in New York City valued at $5 million or more that are not used as a primary residence. As of April 2026, Gov. Hochul and Mayor Mamdani are pushing this tax on non-resident owners to raise ∼$500 million annually, targeting non-residents who underutilize properties.Key Aspects of the Proposed NYC Tax:Target Property: Residential units, particularly luxury condos, acting as a "foot on the ground" (second home) rather than a primary residence.Target Owner: Individuals who live outside the city, do not pay city income tax, but own high-value properties.Value Threshold: Only properties worth $5 million or more are subject to the tax.Rates: Potential sliding scale, with proposals indicating a tax starting around 0.5% on the value over $5 million.Purpose: To fill city budget gaps and ensure owners of vacant, high-value homes contribute to city services.This proposal has faced opposition from the real estate industry, which argues it could affect property values and trigger an exodus of wealthy individuals. It has been debated for several years, dating back to proposals in 2019. A pied-à-terre tax is a proposed annual surcharge on luxury second homes in New York City valued at $5 million or more that are not used as a primary residence. As of April 2026, Gov. Hochul and Mayor Mamdani are pushing this tax on non-resident owners to raise ∼$500 million annually, targeting non-residents who underutilize properties. Key Aspects of the Proposed NYC Tax: Target Property: Residential units, particularly luxury condos, acting as a "foot on the ground" (second home) rather than a primary residence. Target Owner: Individuals who live outside the city, do not pay city income tax, but own high-value properties. Value Threshold: Only properties worth $5 million or more are subject to the tax. Rates: Potential sliding scale, with proposals indicating a tax starting around 0.5% on the value over $5 million. Purpose: To fill city budget gaps and ensure owners of vacant, high-value homes contribute to city services. This proposal has faced opposition from the real estate industry, which argues it could affect property values and trigger an exodus of wealthy individuals. It has been debated for several years, dating back to proposals in 2019.
